semin-durr:4-4.t: His saying: {مِّن جُوعٍ} and {مِّنْ خَوْفٍ}: for cause (li-l-taʿlīl), that is, "because of hunger and fear"; the indefiniteness is for magnification (li-l-taʿẓīm), that is, "from great hunger and great fear". Abū l-Baqāʾ said: "It may be in the position of ḥāl from the object of «أَطْعَمهم»." Nāfiʿ, in one report, concealed the nūn of «مِنْ» before the khāʾ (ikhfāʾ), and likewise before the ghayn; this is a dialect that Sībawayh related.

semin-durr:1-1.t:
His saying: {لإِيلاَفِ قُرَيْشٍ}: concerning what this lām is attached to, there are several views. The first: that it is what is in the preceding sūra, namely His saying {فَجَعَلَهُمْ كَعَصْفٍ} [al-Fīl: 5]. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "This is like enjambment (al-taḍmīn) in poetry", which is that the meaning of one verse depends on the one before it with a dependence that is sound only through it. In the codex of Ubayy the two are a single sūra without a break. It is reported from ʿUmar that he recited them in the second rakʿa of the sunset prayer, having recited {والتين} in the first. End of quotation. Abū l-Ḥasan al-Akhfash held this view, except that al-Ḥawfī said: "A group rejected this view, because if it were so, «لإِيلافِ» would be part of the sūra «ألم تَرَ», yet the unanimous agreement of all on the separation between the two shows that it is not so."
The second: that it is implied, the implied form being "we did that", that is, the destruction of the Companions of the Elephant, "for the familiarity (īlāf) of Quraysh". It was also said that the implied form is «اعْجَبوا» ("marvel!"). The third: that it is His saying «فَلْيَعْبُدوا». The fāʾ entered only because of the sense of condition in the sentence, that is: "if they do not worship Him for all His other favours, let them worship Him for their familiarity, for it is the most evident of His favours to them." Al-Zamakhsharī said this, and it is the view of al-Khalīl before him.
Ibn ʿĀmir read «لإِلافِ» without a yāʾ before the second lām, and the others read «لإِيلافِ» with a yāʾ before it. All agreed on keeping the yāʾ in the second, which is «إيلافِهِمْ». Among the curious things that occurred with these two words is that the readers differed on the dropping and keeping of the yāʾ in the first, although the codices agree on its being written, and they agreed on keeping the yāʾ in the second, although the codices agree on its being dropped in writing. This is the clearest proof that the readers follow the transmitted report and the narration and not merely the script.
As for the reading of Ibn ʿĀmir, there are two views on it. The first: that it is a maṣdar of the triliteral «alifa»; one says "alif-tuhu ilāfan", like "katabtuhu kitāban"; one says "alif-tuhu ilfan" and "ilāfan". The poet combined the two in his saying:
4647 - زَعَمْتُمْ أنَّ إخْوَتَكُمْ قُرَيْشٌ ... لهم إلْفٌ وليس لكُمْ إلافُ
(You claimed that your brothers are Quraysh; they have familiarity (ilf), and you have no familiarity (ilāf).)
The second: that it is the maṣdar of the quadriliteral «ālafa», like "qātala, qitālan". Al-Zamakhsharī said: "that is, for the association (muʾālafa) of Quraysh."
As for the reading of the others, it is the maṣdar of the quadriliteral «ālafa» on the pattern of «akrama»; one says "ālaftuhu, uʾlifuhu, īlāfan". The poet said:
4648 - مِنَ المُؤْلِفاتِ الرَّمْلِ أَدْماءُ حُرَّةٍ ... شعاعُ الضُّحى في مَتْنِها يَتَوضَّحُ
(From among the sand-dwelling does, a pure white noble she-camel; the rays of the forenoon show clear on her back.)
ʿĀṣim in one report read «إإْلافِهم» with two hamzas, the first with kasra and the second quiescent. This is irregular, because in such a case the second must be changed into a homogeneous letter, as in «īmān». It is also reported from him with two hamzas, both with kasra, followed by a quiescent yāʾ. This was explained as the second hamza's kasra having been lengthened so that a yāʾ was generated from it; this is more irregular than the first. Abū l-Baqāʾ transmitted something yet more irregular than it, saying: "with a hamza with kasra, followed by a quiescent yāʾ, followed by a hamza with kasra; this is remote. Its explanation is that he lengthened the kasra, from which the yāʾ arose, and he intended thereby to separate the two hamzas, like the alif in {أَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ} [al-Baqara: 6]."
Abū Jaʿfar read «لإِلْفِ قُرَيْشٍ» on the pattern of «qird». It was already mentioned that it is a maṣdar of «alifa», as in:
4649 -. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... لهم إلْفٌ وليس لكم إلافُ
(. . . they have familiarity (ilf), and you have no familiarity (ilāf).)
From him too, and from Ibn Kathīr, «إلْفِهم»; and from him too, and from Ibn ʿĀmir, «إلا فِهِمْ» like «kitābihim». And from him also «لِيْلافِ» with a quiescent yāʾ after the lām; this is because when he changed the second hamza he dropped the first, contrary to analogy. ʿIkrima read «لِتَأْلَفْ قُرَيْش» as an imperfect verb, and from him «لِيَأْلَفْ» as an imperative, with the lām with kasra; and from him a fatḥa on it with the imperative, which is a minor dialect.
Quraysh is the name of a tribe. It was said that they are the descendants of al-Naḍr ibn Kināna, and everyone whom al-Naḍr fathered is Qurashī, excluding Kināna; and this is the correct view. It was also said that they are the descendants of Fihr ibn Mālik ibn al-Naḍr ibn Kināna; whoever was not fathered by Fihr is not a Qurashī. Agreement was thus reached that the sons of Fihr are Qurashīs and that Kināna are not Qurashīs; the disagreement was over al-Naḍr and Mālik.
There was disagreement over its derivation, on several lines. The first: that it is from «taqarrush», which is gathering; they were so named because they came together after having been dispersed. The poet said:
4650 - أبونا قُصَيُّ كان يدعى مُجَمِّعاً ... به جَمَّعَ اللَّهُ القبائلَ مِنْ فِهْرِ
(Our father Quṣayy used to be called "the gatherer"; through him Allah gathered the tribes of Fihr.)
The second: that it is from «al-qarsh», which is earning. Quraysh were merchants. One says "qarasha, yaqrishu", that is, he earned. The third: that it is from inspection (al-tafṭīsh). One says "qarrasha yuqarrishu ʿannī", that is, he inspected. Quraysh used to inspect their friends in order to meet their needs. The poet said:
4651 - أيُّها الشامِتُ المُقَرِّشُ عنا ... عند عمروٍ فهَلْ له إبْقاءُ
(O you who gloat and spy on us at ʿAmr's, is there any mercy in him?)
Muʿāwiya asked Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "It was named after a creature of the sea called al-qirsh, which eats and is not eaten, overcomes and is not overcome." And he recited the saying of Tubbaʿ:
4652 - وَقُرَيْشٌ هي التي تَسْكُنُ البَحْ ... رَ سُمِّيَتْ قُرَيْشٌ قُرَيْشَا
تأكلُ الغَثَّ والسَّمينَ ولا تَتْ ... رُكُ فيها لذي جناحَيْنِ رِيشا
هكذا في البلادِ حَيُّ قُرَيْشٍ ... يأكلونَ البلادَ أكْلاً كَميشا
ولهم آخِرَ الزمان نَبيٌّ ... يُكْثِرُ القَتْلَ فيهمُ والخُموشا
(Quraysh is the one that dwells in the sea; Quraysh was named "Quraysh". It eats the lean and the fat, and leaves no feather for any winged creature. So too in the lands the clan of Quraysh devour the lands with a hasty devouring. And at the end of time they will have a prophet who will bring much killing and scratching among them.)
Then Quraysh is either a diminutive of a word with more than three radicals, in which case its diminutive is a diminutive of truncation (taṣghīr tarkhīm), and it was said that the original is «muqrish», or «qārish»; or it is a diminutive of a triliteral such as «al-qarsh». They agreed that it is inflected (maṣrūf) here, the clan being intended by it; had the tribe been intended, it would have been diptote (mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf), as in the saying of the poet:
465 - 3- غَلَبَ المَساميحَ الوليدُ سَماحةً ... وكفى قُرَيْشَ المُعْضِلاتِ وسادَها
(Al-Walīd surpassed the generous in generosity, and spared Quraysh its hard matters, and led them.)
[Translator's note: the verse number is printed as «465 - 3-», evidently 4653.]
Sībawayh said of Maʿadd, Quraysh, Thaqīf and Kināna: "These are for clans; and if you make it a name for tribes, that is permissible and good."
His saying: {إِيلاَفِهِمْ}: an emphasis of the first, a verbal emphasis (tawkīd lafẓī); for this reason it is attached to the pronoun of the one to whom the first was annexed, as you say: "I honoured Zayd for his standing, for his standing" (li-qiyāmi Zayd li-qiyāmihi akramtuhu). Abū l-Baqāʾ parsed it as a badal, but the first is better.
His saying: {رِحْلَةَ}: an object of the maṣdar, the maṣdar being annexed to its agent, that is, "because they became familiar with the journey". The original is "the two journeys of winter and summer", but it was put in the singular because there is no risk of confusion, as in his saying:
4654 - كُلوا في بَعْضِ بطنِكُمُ تَعِفُّوا ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(Eat in part of your bellies, and you will be chaste . . .)
Al-Zamakhsharī said this, and it is open to question, since Sībawayh treats this as poetic licence (ḍarūra), as in his saying:
4655 - حَمامةً بَطْنِ الوادِيَيْنِ تَرَنَّمي ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(O dove of the belly of the two valleys, coo . . .)
It was also said that «رِحْلة» is a generic noun (ism jins); they had four journeys. Some made it a mistake, but it is not so. The majority read it with kasra on the rāʾ, and it is a maṣdar; Abū l-Sammāl read it with ḍamma, and it is the destination to which one journeys.
Al-shitāʾ (winter) has a wāw as its lām (third radical), from their saying «al-shatwa» and «shatā yashtū». They deviated in forming the relative adjective from it, saying «shatawī»; the analogy is «shitāʾī» or «shitāwī», like «kisāʾī» and «kisāwī».
